method.method_draft: Use the magnetic dipole moment of the loop. First read the diagram: the loop lies in the x-y plane, the axle is the dashed vertical line through the middle and is labeled as the fixed axle along the y-axis, and the current arrows show current along the front horizontal side toward +x, along the back/top side toward -x, with the side segments completing a counterclockwise circulation when viewed from +z. From the text, use that the loop is a square current loop that can rotate about the y-axis and the requested torque is clockwise as shown. Apply the right-hand rule to the current direction to get the loop’s magnetic moment μ in the +z direction. Then use the torque law τ = μ × B. The clockwise torque shown about the y-axis corresponds to τ in the +y direction. Since μ is +z, choose B so that +z × B = +y; this requires B in the +x direction.

method.method_draft: Use magnetic forces on the individual wire segments. From the diagram, read that the front horizontal segment carries current to the right (+x), the back/top horizontal segment carries current to the left (-x), the right slanted side carries current toward +y, and the left slanted side carries current toward -y; the axle is the central y-axis. From the text, the loop is in the x-y plane and must experience a clockwise torque about that y-axis. Test a magnetic field along +x. The front and back horizontal segments are parallel or antiparallel to B, so they feel no magnetic force. On the right side, I dl is along +y, so F = I dl × B gives +y × +x = -z, a downward force. On the left side, I dl is along -y, so -y × +x = +z, an upward force. The left side rising and right side falling is a clockwise rotation in the x-z view, and both forces give torque about the axle in the same +y sense. Therefore B should point in the +x direction.
